questions.stem: Which hormone lowers blood calcium by inhibiting intestinal Ca²⁺ absorption and increasing renal Ca²⁺ excretion?
questions.explanation: Per the lecture, glucocorticoids decrease blood Ca²⁺ by inhibiting intestinal absorption and increasing renal excretion. A: Calcitonin also lowers Ca²⁺, but by inhibiting osteoclasts. B: GH raises Ca²⁺ by increasing intestinal absorption. D: PTH raises Ca²⁺ (bone resorption, renal reabsorption, calcitriol). E: Calcitriol raises Ca²⁺ by increasing intestinal absorption.

questions.stem: A signal opens Ca²⁺ channels for only milliseconds, yet local cytosolic Ca²⁺ rises 10–20-fold. What makes this possible?

options.A: A ~10,000-fold inward Ca²⁺ gradient across PM and ER
options.B: Ca²⁺-binding proteins release their bound Ca²⁺
options.D: Ca²⁺ diffuses freely across the lipid bilayer
options.E: Ca²⁺ enters the cytosol by primary active transport

questions.explanation: Cytosolic Ca²⁺ (~10⁻⁷ M) is ~10,000-fold below ECF and ER Ca²⁺ (~10⁻³ M), so Ca²⁺ rushes into the cytosol as soon as channels open. B: Ca²⁺-binding proteins buffer (take up) Ca²⁺ and blunt the rise. C: Mitochondria take up Ca²⁺ as a removal mechanism. D: Ca²⁺ needs channels to cross. E: Entry is passive through channels; pumps remove Ca²⁺.

questions.stem: In a ventricular myocyte, which event directly triggers release of Ca²⁺ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum?

options.A: IP₃ binding to IP₃ receptors on the SR
options.B: Ca²⁺ entering via L-type channels and opening RyR2

questions.explanation: Trigger Ca²⁺ through L-type channels (LTCC) in the T-tubule opens RyR2 on the SR (calcium-induced calcium release). A: IP₃-gated channels release ER Ca²⁺ in Gq signaling, not the cardiac trigger. C: Phospholamban (PLB) regulates SERCA2a reuptake, i.e. relaxation. D: NCX removes Ca²⁺ during relaxation. E: Troponin binding follows SR release.

questions.stem: Which ECG change and symptom pair fit a plasma calcium of 14 mg/dL?
questions.explanation: Hypercalcemia (depressive effects above ~12 mg/dL) shortens QT and depresses nerves and gut smooth muscle (constipation, sluggish reflexes). A: QT prolongation and tetany suggest hypocalcemia. B: QT shortens in hypercalcemia. C: Tetany is hypocalcemia (~6 mg/dL). E: QT shortens and reflexes become sluggish.

questions.stem: Two days after total thyroidectomy, a 45-year-old woman has perioral tingling and carpal spasm when a BP cuff is inflated. Which change underlies her neuromuscular findings?

options.B: Excess PTH acting on motor neurons
options.C: Loss of calcitonin's effect on nerves

questions.explanation: Inadvertent parathyroid removal → low PTH → hypocalcemia → increased neuronal Na⁺ permeability → easy AP initiation (tetany). A: K⁺ channel block isn't the lecture's mechanism. B: PTH is low, not high. C: Calcitonin loss doesn't cause tetany. D: The problem is low ECF Ca²⁺.

questions.stem: Which protein lowers cytosolic Ca²⁺ by ATP-driven pumping into an intracellular store?
questions.explanation: SERCA is the ER/SR Ca²⁺ pump (regulated by phospholamban in the heart). A: PMCA uses ATP but pumps Ca²⁺ out of the cell. B: NCX uses the Na⁺ gradient to move Ca²⁺ out of the cell. D: Mitochondrial import is driven by the H⁺ gradient, not ATP directly. E: Binding proteins buffer Ca²⁺; they don't transport it.

questions.stem: A researcher wants to measure cytosolic Ca²⁺ with a fluorescent indicator rather than a Ca²⁺-sensitive photoprotein. Which should she use?
questions.explanation: Fura-2 and Fluo-3 are fluorescent Ca²⁺ markers. A: Aequorin is the jellyfish photoprotein, the other measurement method. C: Ryanodine is the plant alkaloid that names the SR release channel. D: TTX blocks Na⁺ channels. E: IP₃ releases ER Ca²⁺; it doesn't measure it.

questions.stem: Which calcium-balance pattern is expected in a healthy 10-year-old during a growth spurt?

options.A: Absorption exceeds urinary excretion; net bone deposition
options.B: Urinary excretion exceeds absorption; net bone deposition
options.C: Urinary excretion exceeds absorption; net bone resorption
options.D: Absorption equals urinary excretion; no net bone change
options.E: Absorption exceeds urinary excretion; net bone resorption

questions.explanation: Growing children are in positive Ca²⁺ balance: intestinal absorption > urinary excretion, and the excess is deposited in bone. B: Negative balance can't fund net deposition. C: Negative balance, seen in pregnancy and lactation. D: Describes a stable adult. E: A positive balance goes into bone, not out of it.
